hints: Trace the whole chain in order from the N terminal end to the C terminal end and mark every light oval, as these are the only non-polar amino acids that can be part of a cut site.
A cut happens only where a light oval sits directly next to any darker or white shape, so a non-polar next to a non-polar, or a polar next to a polar, is never cut.
walkthrough:
**Sort the shapes by type**

Think like the enzyme. It only cares about one thing: is this amino acid non-polar or not?

Light oval = non-polar, like Ala, Val, Phe, Leu, Met, Pro. All other shapes = polar of some kind: dark square is polar basic, white hexagon is polar acidic, grey hexagon is polar.

**Find every cut site**

Walk along the chain from N to C and check each peptide bond between neighbours.

Cut rule: cut if one side is non-polar and the other side is any polar.
$$ \text{fragments} = \text{number of cuts} + 1 $$
You will find 16 such NP to P junctions, for example Thr to Ala, Ala to Lys, Lys to Phe, Phe to Glu, His to Met, Met to Asp, and so on all the way to Val to His.

**Count peptides versus single amino acids**

16 cuts splits the long chain into 17 pieces.

A single amino acid appears when both bonds around it are cut, or it is a very short isolated piece. This happens 4 times: Lys, Phe, Met and Leu are each trapped between two cuts. The remaining pieces are longer:
$$ 17 - 4 = 13 \text{ small peptides} $$
So you get 13 small peptides and 4 single amino acids.

options.A: Too low. It misses most NP to P junctions along the long chain, there are far more than 5 or 6 cuts.
options.B: Too low. Counting only some obvious non-polar blocks like Ala and Met misses other isolated cuts such as Leu, Pro, Val, Phe and Thr to Ala.
options.C: Close but undercounts by one cut. Missing the Thr to Ala cut near the N terminal end loses one peptide and one single amino acid.
options.D: Correct. 16 NP to P bonds are hydrolysed to give 17 fragments, which are 13 small peptides plus 4 single amino acids (Lys, Phe, Met, Leu).
